claim: miR-142 and miR-150 are upregulated in human breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs) as compared to the non-tumorigenic breast cancer cells.
source: We previously reported that miR-142 and miR-150 are upregulated in human breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs) as compared to the non-tumorigenic breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors, supported by citation to their prior work (Shimono et al., 2009).

claim: miR-142 efficiently recruits the APC mRNA to an RNA-induced silencing complex.
source: In this study, we report that miR-142 efficiently recruits the APC mRNA to an RNA-induced silencing complex
evidence: Supported by Ago IP/microarray experiments shown in Figure 1 and described in the Results section.

claim: miR-142 activates the canonical WNT signaling pathway in an APC-suppression dependent manner.
source: In this study, we report that miR-142 efficiently recruits the APC mRNA to an RNA-induced silencing complex, activates the canonical WNT signaling pathway in an APC-suppression dependent manner
evidence: Supported by TOPFlash/FOPFlash reporter assays and rescue experiments with APC mutant plasmids shown in Figure 3.

claim: miR-142 activates the expression of miR-150.
source: In this study, we report that miR-142 efficiently recruits the APC mRNA to an RNA-induced silencing complex, activates the canonical WNT signaling pathway in an APC-suppression dependent manner, and activates the expression of miR-150.
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR data and chromatin IP experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Enforced expression of miR-142 in normal mouse mammary stem cells resulted in the regeneration of hyperproliferative mammary glands in vivo.
source: Enforced expression of miR-142 or miR-150 in normal mouse mammary stem cells resulted in the regeneration of hyperproliferative mammary glands in vivo.
evidence: Supported by mammary transplantation experiments and histological analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Enforced expression of miR-150 in normal mouse mammary stem cells resulted in the regeneration of hyperproliferative mammary glands in vivo.
source: Enforced expression of miR-142 or miR-150 in normal mouse mammary stem cells resulted in the regeneration of hyperproliferative mammary glands in vivo.
evidence: Supported by mammary transplantation experiments and histological analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Knockdown of endogenous miR-142 effectively suppressed organoid formation by BCSCs.
source: Knockdown of endogenous miR-142 effectively suppressed organoid formation by BCSCs and slowed tumor growth initiated by human BCSCs in vivo.
evidence: Supported by organoid formation assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Knockdown of endogenous miR-142 slowed tumor growth initiated by human BCSCs in vivo.
source: Knockdown of endogenous miR-142 effectively suppressed organoid formation by BCSCs and slowed tumor growth initiated by human BCSCs in vivo.
evidence: Supported by xenograft tumor growth experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are evolutionally conserved small non-coding RNAs that regulate the translation of mRNAs.
source: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are evolutionally conserved small non-coding RNAs that regulate the translation of mRNAs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about miRNAs.

claim: miRNAs are recruited to an RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) and bind to the seed sequence within the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of target mRNAs.
source: They are recruited to an RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) and bind to the seed sequence within the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of target mRNAs, leading to destabilization and/or translational suppression of the target mRNAs (Bartel, 2009).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: miRNA binding to target mRNAs leads to destabilization and/or translational suppression of the target mRNAs.
source: They are recruited to an RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) and bind to the seed sequence within the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of target mRNAs, leading to destabilization and/or translational suppression of the target mRNAs (Bartel, 2009).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The Ago IP/microarray method enables comprehensive identification of miRNA-target genes in an unbiased manner.
source: The immunopurification (IP) of Argonaute (Ago), a central component of the RISC in the human and mouse, followed by microarray analyses (Ago IP/microarray method) makes it possible to isolate any Ago-associated miRNAs and mRNAs without relying on the mechanism of regulation (i.e. mRNA decay or translational suppression), or sequence conservation, enabling a comprehensive identification of the miRNA-target genes in an unbiased manner.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by citations to Hendrickson et al., 2008, 2009.

claim: The Ago IP/microarray method provides quantitative information about the mRNAs that are regulated by miRNAs.
source: This provides quantitative information about the mRNAs that are regulated by miRNAs (Hendrickson et al., 2008, 2009).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by citations.

claim: miRNAs are able to regulate the expression of hundreds of target mRNAs simultaneously.
source: miRNAs are able to regulate the expression of hundreds of target mRNAs simultaneously and control a variety of cell functions including cell proliferation, stem cell maintenance, and differentiation (Lewis et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: miRNAs control a variety of cell functions including cell proliferation, stem cell maintenance, and differentiation.
source: miRNAs are able to regulate the expression of hundreds of target mRNAs simultaneously and control a variety of cell functions including cell proliferation, stem cell maintenance, and differentiation (Lewis et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A CD44+ CD24−/low lineage− population of human breast cancer cells is enriched for the ability to drive tumor formation in a mouse xenograft model.
source: We previously identified a human breast cancer stem cell (BCSC) population (a CD44+ CD24−/low lineage− population of human breast cancer cells) that in many human breast tumors is enriched for the ability to drive tumor formation in a mouse xenograft model as compared to the remaining non-tumorigenic cancer cells (NTG cells) within the same breast tumor (Al-Hajj et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a previous finding by the authors supported by citation.

claim: 37 miRNAs are differentially expressed between human BCSCs and NTG cells.
source: Comprehensive analyses of the expression profile of 466 miRNAs revealed that 37 miRNAs are differentially expressed between the human BCSCs and NTG cells (Shimono et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a previous finding by the authors supported by citation.

claim: miR-200c and miR-183 are downregulated in human BCSCs.
source: Among them, both miR-200c and miR-183 are downregulated in the human BCSCs and suppress the protein expression of the stem cell self-renewal gene, BMI1, and miR-200c suppresses the protein expression of the EMT regulator ZEB1 (Shimono et al., 2009; Wellner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a previous finding supported by citations.

claim: miR-200c and miR-183 suppress the protein expression of the stem cell self-renewal gene, BMI1.
source: Among them, both miR-200c and miR-183 are downregulated in the human BCSCs and suppress the protein expression of the stem cell self-renewal gene, BMI1, and miR-200c suppresses the protein expression of the EMT regulator ZEB1 (Shimono et al., 2009; Wellner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a previous finding supported by citations.

claim: miR-200c suppresses the protein expression of the EMT regulator ZEB1.
source: Among them, both miR-200c and miR-183 are downregulated in the human BCSCs and suppress the protein expression of the stem cell self-renewal gene, BMI1, and miR-200c suppresses the protein expression of the EMT regulator ZEB1 (Shimono et al., 2009; Wellner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a previous finding supported by citations.

claim: Enforced expression of miR-200c can strongly suppress the tumor formation driven by human BCSCs.
source: Enforced expression of miR-200c can strongly suppress the tumor formation driven by human BCSCs and the mammary ducts formation by normal mammary stem cells in vivo, suggesting that miR-200c is a regulator of normal mammary and BCSCs.
evidence: This is a previous finding supported by citation to Shimono et al., 2009.

claim: Enforced expression of miR-200c can suppress mammary ducts formation by normal mammary stem cells in vivo.
source: Enforced expression of miR-200c can strongly suppress the tumor formation driven by human BCSCs and the mammary ducts formation by normal mammary stem cells in vivo, suggesting that miR-200c is a regulator of normal mammary and BCSCs.
evidence: This is a previous finding supported by citation to Shimono et al., 2009.

claim: miR-200c is a regulator of normal mammary and BCSCs.
source: Enforced expression of miR-200c can strongly suppress the tumor formation driven by human BCSCs and the mammary ducts formation by normal mammary stem cells in vivo, suggesting that miR-200c is a regulator of normal mammary and BCSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional effects of miR-200c.

claim: The expression of miR-142, miR-150, and miR-155 are upregulated in human BCSCs.
source: On the other hand, the expression of miRNAs, such as miR-142, miR-150, and miR-155, are upregulated in human BCSCs (Shimono et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a previous finding supported by citation.

claim: miR-155 was originally identified as a product of the oncogenic BIC gene locus in B cell lymphoma.
source: Among them, miR-155 was originally identified as a product of the oncogenic BIC gene locus in B cell lymphoma (Eis et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Abnormal proliferation and myelodysplasia are seen when miR-155 expression is sustained in the blood system.
source: Abnormal proliferation and myelodysplasia are seen when miR-155 expression is sustained in the blood system (O'Connell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: miR-155 functions as an oncogenic miRNA in various cancers, including leukemia and breast cancers.
source: Furthermore, miR-155 functions as an oncogenic miRNA in various cancers, including leukemia and breast cancers (Czyzyk-Krzeska and Zhang, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Dysregulation of miR-142 and miR-150 are reported in leukemia, gastric and lung cancers.
source: Dysregulation of miR-142 and miR-150 are reported in leukemia, gastric and lung cancers, but their roles in breast cancer or BCSCs are not elucidated.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claim: The roles of miR-142 and miR-150 in breast cancer or BCSCs are not elucidated.
source: Dysregulation of miR-142 and miR-150 are reported in leukemia, gastric and lung cancers, but their roles in breast cancer or BCSCs are not elucidated.
evidence: This establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: miR-142 is involved in hematopoiesis, immune responses, and T cell differentiation.
source: miR-142 is involved in hematopoiesis, immune responses, and T cell differentiation (Chen and Lodish, 2005; Ramkissoon et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2007; Visone et al., 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: miR-142 is upregulated in bronchoalveolar stem cells.
source: miR-142 is involved in hematopoiesis, immune responses, and T cell differentiation (Chen and Lodish, 2005; Ramkissoon et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2007; Visone et al., 2009) and is upregulated in bronchoalveolar stem cells (Qian et al., 2008)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: miR-142 might have a role in the regulation of tissue stem cells.
source: and is upregulated in bronchoalveolar stem cells (Qian et al., 2008), suggesting it might have a role in the regulation of tissue stem cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern of miR-142 in stem cells.

claim: miR-142 is upregulated in human T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
source: miR-142 is upregulated in human T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Lv et al., 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: miR-142 is downregulated in acute myeloid leukemia.
source: but is downregulated in acute myeloid leukemia (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: miR-150 is upregulated in adult T-cell leukemia cells.
source: miR-150 is upregulated in adult T-cell leukemia cells (Bellon et al., 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: miR-150 is upregulated in gastric cancers.
source: miR-150 is upregulated in adult T-cell leukemia cells (Bellon et al., 2009), gastric cancers (Wu et al., 2010)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: miR-150 is upregulated in lung cancers.
source: miR-150 is upregulated in adult T-cell leukemia cells (Bellon et al., 2009), gastric cancers (Wu et al., 2010), and lung cancers (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The canonical Wnt pathway signal is transduced by β-catenin.
source: The canonical Wnt pathway signal is transduced by β-catenin and plays a critical role in many adult stem cells, including those of the breast and intestine (Reya and Clevers, 2005; Zeng and Nusse, 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The canonical Wnt pathway plays a critical role in many adult stem cells, including those of the breast and intestine.
source: The canonical Wnt pathway signal is transduced by β-catenin and plays a critical role in many adult stem cells, including those of the breast and intestine (Reya and Clevers, 2005; Zeng and Nusse, 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Normal physiological regulators of stem cell functions might be 'hijacked' in cancer.
source: The fact that some cancer cells share the extended self-renewal ability with normal stem cells, and that the canonical Wnt signaling pathway is implicated in both stem cell self-renewal and cancer suggests that normal physiological regulators of stem cell functions might be 'hijacked' in cancer (Reya and Clevers, 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation and inference from shared properties.

claim: c-Myc and cyclin D1 are putative transcriptional targets of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway.
source: A variety of putative transcriptional targets of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, such as c-Myc and cyclin D1, are identified (He et al., 1998; Shtutman et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) is a component of the destruction complex that destabilizes β-catenin.
source: Adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) is a component of the destruction complex that destabilizes β-catenin and suppresses the activity of the canonical WNT signaling pathway.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: APC suppresses the activity of the canonical WNT signaling pathway.
source: Adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) is a component of the destruction complex that destabilizes β-catenin and suppresses the activity of the canonical WNT signaling pathway.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Mutations in the APC gene are the most commonly known acquired genetic change for the aberrant activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway in human colon cancers.
source: In human colon cancers, mutations in the APC gene are the most commonly known acquired genetic change for the aberrant activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway during the tumor development and progression (Kinzler et al., 1991; Nishisho et al., 1991; Cottrell et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: APC gene mutations play an important role in the initiation step of colon tumorigenesis.
source: In a model for the stepwise progression of the colon tumorigenesis, APC gene mutations play an important role in the initiation step followed by successive mutations in other genes, including K-Ras and p53 (Fearon and Vogelstein, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: During clonal progression, dysregulation of downstream β-catenin targets, such as c-Myc, can relieve colon cancer cells of their dependence on β-catenin signaling.
source: During clonal progression, dysregulation of downstream β-catenin targets, such as c-Myc, can relieve colon cancer cells of their dependence on β-catenin signaling (van de Wetering et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The expression of APC is widely observed in many tissues, including lung, liver, kidney, and mammary tissue.
source: The expression of APC is not limited to the intestine but is widely observed in many other tissues, including lung, liver, kidney, and mammary tissue.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: The role of the suppression of APC and the activation of the canonical WNT signaling in the tumor initiation process of tissues other than the colon largely remains unknown.
source: However, the role of the suppression of APC and the activation of the canonical WNT signaling in the tumor initiation process of the tissues other than the colon largely remains unknown, because APC mutations are less frequent in tumors originating from these tissues.
evidence: This establishes a knowledge gap.

claim: Recent data from the TCGA reveals an ∼2% incidence of APC mutations in breast cancer.
source: For example, recent data from the TCGA reveals an ∼2% incidence of APC mutations in breast cancer (the TCGA Research Network: http://cancergenome.nih.gov/).
evidence: This is data from TCGA cited as a source.

claim: APC promoter methylation occurs in 36–54% of human breast cancers.
source: Dampening of APC inhibition of β-catenin appears to be more often due to promoter methylation (36–54%) and loss of heterozygosity (LOH) (23%) than to somatically acquired APC mutations (∼2%) in human breast cancers (Sarrio et al., 2003; Jin et al., 2001; Banerji et al., 2012; The cancer genome atlas network 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss of heterozygosity (LOH) of APC occurs in 23% of human breast cancers.
source: Dampening of APC inhibition of β-catenin appears to be more often due to promoter methylation (36–54%) and loss of heterozygosity (LOH) (23%) than to somatically acquired APC mutations (∼2%) in human breast cancers (Sarrio et al., 2003; Jin et al., 2001; Banerji et al., 2012; The cancer genome atlas network 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The presence of APC promoter methylation and LOH are independent of tumor size or stage.
source: but the presence of the APC promoter methylation and LOH are independent of tumor size or stage (Jin et al., 2001; Sarrio et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: APC mutations in breast cancers are typically found at sites distinct from the APC mutation cluster region in colorectal cancers.
source: The APC mutations in breast cancers are typically found at sites distinct from the APC mutation cluster region in colorectal cancers and are much more frequently seen in advanced than early stage breast cancers (Furuuchi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: APC mutations are much more frequently seen in advanced than early stage breast cancers.
source: The APC mutations in breast cancers are typically found at sites distinct from the APC mutation cluster region in colorectal cancers and are much more frequently seen in advanced than early stage breast cancers (Furuuchi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: APC is targeted by miRNAs, such as miR-27, miR-155, and miR-142.
source: On the other hand, APC is targeted by the miRNAs, such as miR-27, miR-155, and miR-142 (Lu et al., 2009; Wang and Xu, 2010; Liu et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: miRNAs that target APC may regulate the aberrant activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway for the initiation of human breast cancers.
source: These observations suggest that in addition to LOH, promoter methylation, and the APC mutations, miRNAs that target APC may regulate the aberrant activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway for the initiation of human breast cancers, the enhancement of niche independence, and the aberrant proliferation of the human BCSCs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observations.

claim: miRNAs that target APC may enhance niche independence of human BCSCs.
source: These observations suggest that in addition to LOH, promoter methylation, and the APC mutations, miRNAs that target APC may regulate the aberrant activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway for the initiation of human breast cancers, the enhancement of niche independence, and the aberrant proliferation of the human BCSCs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observations.

claim: miRNAs that target APC may regulate the aberrant proliferation of human BCSCs.
source: These observations suggest that in addition to LOH, promoter methylation, and the APC mutations, miRNAs that target APC may regulate the aberrant activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway for the initiation of human breast cancers, the enhancement of niche independence, and the aberrant proliferation of the human BCSCs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observations.

claim: The efficiency of miR-142-dependent recruitment of specific mRNAs to the RISC complex correlated well with the types of miRNA seed matches.
source: The efficiency of the miR142-dependent and miR-150-dependent recruitment of specific mRNAs to the RISC complex correlated well with the types of miRNA seed matches: mRNAs with the 8mer match were most efficiently enriched, followed by those with the 7mer-m8, 7mer-1A, and 6mer sites (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the Ago IP/microarray data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: mRNAs with the 8mer match were most efficiently enriched in RISC by miR-142, followed by those with the 7mer-m8, 7mer-1A, and 6mer sites.
source: The efficiency of the miR142-dependent and miR-150-dependent recruitment of specific mRNAs to the RISC complex correlated well with the types of miRNA seed matches: mRNAs with the 8mer match were most efficiently enriched, followed by those with the 7mer-m8, 7mer-1A, and 6mer sites (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the Ago IP/microarray data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both miR-142 and miR-150 were predicted to target the APC mRNA by a computer algorithm.
source: Although both miR-142 and miR-150 were predicted to target the APC mRNA by a computer algorithm, the results of the Ago IP/microarray experiments showed that the APC mRNA was efficiently recruited to RISC by miR-142, and that it was hardly recruited to RISC by miR-150 (Figure 1A—source data 1–4).
evidence: This is stated as a computational prediction.

claim: The APC mRNA was efficiently recruited to RISC by miR-142.
source: Although both miR-142 and miR-150 were predicted to target the APC mRNA by a computer algorithm, the results of the Ago IP/microarray experiments showed that the APC mRNA was efficiently recruited to RISC by miR-142, and that it was hardly recruited to RISC by miR-150 (Figure 1A—source data 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by Ago IP/microarray data.

claim: The APC mRNA was hardly recruited to RISC by miR-150.
source: Although both miR-142 and miR-150 were predicted to target the APC mRNA by a computer algorithm, the results of the Ago IP/microarray experiments showed that the APC mRNA was efficiently recruited to RISC by miR-142, and that it was hardly recruited to RISC by miR-150 (Figure 1A—source data 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by Ago IP/microarray data.

claim: The APC mRNA was strongly recruited to Ago by miR-142 among genes associated with the activity of the WNT signaling pathway.
source: Among the genes associated with the activity of the WNT signaling pathway, we found that the APC mRNA was strongly recruited to Ago by miR-142 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Ago IP enrichment data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The abundance of the APC mRNA was reduced in the miR-142-transfected HEK293T cells.
source: In the parallel experiments, amplified RNAs from the whole cell lysate from HEK293T cells transfected with or without the miR-142 precursor were labeled and hybridized to the HEEBO microarrays. The results showed that the abundance of the APC mRNA was consistently reduced in the miR-142-transfected HEK293T cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data.

claim: Co-transfection of the miR-142 precursor suppressed the luciferase activity by 37% when the 3′ UTR of the APC mRNA was included in the luciferase transcript.
source: We observed that when the 3′ UTR of the APC mRNA was included in the luciferase transcript, co-transfection of the miR-142 precursor suppressed the luciferase activity by 37% (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mutations of the two nucleotides within the predicted target site for miR-142-3p in the 3′ UTR of the APC mRNA significantly weakened the ability of miR-142 to suppress the luciferase activity.
source: Mutations of the two nucleotides within the predicted target site for miR-142-3p in the 3′ UTR of the APC mRNA significantly weakened the ability of miR-142 to suppress the luciferase activity (Figure 2A,B)
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data with mutant constructs shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: miR-142 specifically targets the predicted seed sequence in the 3′ UTR of the APC mRNA to suppress the translation of the APC mRNA.
source: Mutations of the two nucleotides within the predicted target site for miR-142-3p in the 3′ UTR of the APC mRNA significantly weakened the ability of miR-142 to suppress the luciferase activity (Figure 2A,B), suggesting that miR-142 specifically targets the predicted seed sequence in the 3′ UTR of the APC mRNA to suppress the translation of the APC mRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis experiment results.

claim: The protein level of APC was decreased in the HEK293T cells expressing miR-142 after 6 days.
source: Western blot analyses showed that, after 6 days, the protein level of APC was decreased in the HEK293T cells expressing miR-142 when compared to the control precursor transfected cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The protein level of APC was reduced in both MCF7 and MDA-MB-231 cells transfected with the miR-142 precursor.
source: To confirm our findings, breast cancer cells, such as MCF7 and MDA-MB-231 cells, were transfected with the miR-142 precursor. We found that the protein level of APC was reduced in both MCF7 and MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The protein level of APC was elevated in HEK293T, MDA-MB-231, and MCF7 cells transduced with the anti-miR-142-3p vector.
source: Next, the expression of miR-142-3p was knocked down using an anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus in the HEK293T, MDA-MB-231, and MCF7 cells which expressed miR-142 at low levels. We found that the protein level of APC was elevated in HEK293T, MDA-MB-231, and MCF7 cells transduced with the anti-miR-142-3p vector (Figure 2E and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: miR-142 effectively targets the APC mRNA and reduces the protein level of APC in cells including human breast cancer cells.
source: These results suggest that miR-142 effectively targets the APC mRNA and reduces the protein level of APC in the cells including the human breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot and luciferase assay results.

claim: The normalized TOPFlash/FOPFlash ratio of the luciferase activities increased by 364% in the miR-142 transfected HEK293T cells compared to that in the control precursor transfected cells when stimulated with LiCl.
source: HEK293T cells were transfected with the miR-142 precursor and incubated with 20 mM lithium chloride (LiCl) for 6 hr to stimulate the canonical WNT signaling pathway (by inhibiting the activity of the glycogen synthase kinase 3) (van Noort et al., 2002). We found that the normalized TOPFlash/FOPFlash ratio of the luciferase activities increased by 364% in the miR-142 transfected HEK293T cells compared to that in the control precursor transfected cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by TOPFlash/FOPFlash reporter assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The elevation of the normalized TOPFlash/FOPFlash value in the miR-142 transfected cells was observed by the stimulation with Wnt3A.
source: In accordance with this result, the elevation of the normalized TOPFlash/FOPFlash value in the miR-142 transfected cells was observed by the stimulation with Wnt3A (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by TOPFlash/FOPFlash reporter assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Co-transfection of pCMV-Neo-APC mutant plasmid significantly suppressed the normalized TOPFlash/FOPFlash value to an intensity comparable to that of the control miRNA precursor transfected cells.
source: The co-transfection of the control plasmid, pCMV-Neo-Control, or the pCMV-Neo-APC plasmid that contains miR-142-3p targeted sequence within the 3′ UTR region, did not affect the ability of miR-142 to elevate the normalized TOPFlash/FOPFlash value. On the contrary, co-transfection of pCMV-Neo-APC mutant plasmid significantly suppressed the normalized TOPFlash/FOPFlash value to an intensity comparable to that of the control miRNA precursor transfected cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by TOPFlash/FOPFlash reporter assay data with rescue experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The activation of canonical WNT signaling pathway by miR-142 is mostly mediated by the ability of miR-142 to reduce the protein level of APC.
source: These results suggest that the activation of canonical WNT signaling pathway by miR-142 is mostly mediated by the ability of miR-142 to reduce the protein level of APC.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment results.

claim: The GFP-positive cells infected with the control lentivirus formed round-shaped organoids in 7 days in the MLTV-Wnt-1 tumor model.
source: The GFP-positive cells infected with the control lentivirus formed round-shaped organoids in 7 days (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Most of the MLTV-Wnt-1 mammary CSCs infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentiviruses failed to form the round-shaped organoids.
source: In contrast, most of the cells infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentiviruses failed to form the round-shaped organoids (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The number of the GFP positive organoids was significantly decreased when the mammary CSCs were infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus.
source: The number of the GFP positive organoids was significantly decreased when the mammary CSCs were infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: miR-142-3p is an important regulator of the organoid formation ability in murine mammary CSCs.
source: These results suggest that miR-142-3p is an important regulator of the organoid formation ability in murine mammary CSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the organoid formation assay results.

claim: The GFP positive cells infected with the control lentivirus formed round-shaped organoids in 10 days in human BCSCs.
source: The GFP positive cells infected with the control lentivirus formed round-shaped organoids in 10 days (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Most of the human BCSCs infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentiviruses failed to form the round-shaped organoids.
source: In contrast, most of the cells infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentiviruses failed to form the round-shaped organoids (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The number of the GFP positive organoids was significantly decreased when the human BCSCs were infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus.
source: The number of the GFP positive organoids was significantly decreased when the human BCSCs were infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The percentage of the EdU-positive cells in the GFP-positive organoids was significantly reduced when the human BCSCs were infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus.
source: We found that the percentage of the EdU-positive cells in the GFP-positive organoids was significantly reduced when the human BCSCs were infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The percentage of the annexin V-positive cells in the GFP positive organoids was significantly increased when the human BCSCs were infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus.
source: We found that the percentage of the annexin V-positive cells in the GFP positive organoids was significantly increased when the human BCSCs were infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: miR-142 critically affects the clonogenic properties of the BCSCs by regulating the proliferation and apoptosis of the breast cancer cells.
source: These results suggest that miR-142 critically affects the clonogenic properties of the BCSCs by regulating the proliferation and apoptosis of the breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the EdU and annexin V staining results.

claim: The promoter region of miR-150 contains a potential β-catenin/TCF transcription factor binding site.
source: Because the promoter region of miR-150 contains a potential β-catenin/TCF transcription factor binding site (Figure 5A), we investigated whether miR-150 expression is regulated by the canonical WNT signaling pathway.
evidence: This is shown in the schematic in Figure 5A.

claim: The anti-β-catenin antibody selectively enriched DNA fragments containing the potential β-catenin/TCF binding site within the promoter of the miR-150 precursor.
source: HEK293T cells were stimulated with 20 mM LiCl for 7 hr, then crosslinked with formaldehyde, and chromatin immunoprecipitation was performed either with an antibody against β-catenin or, as a control, with mouse IgG. The anti-β-catenin antibody selectively enriched DNA fragments containing the potential β-catenin/TCF binding site within the promoter of the miR-150 precursor (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin IP data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The expression of miR-142 was able to upregulate the expression of miR-150 in human breast cancer MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Then, using semi-quantitative real-time PCR, we found that the expression of miR-142 was able to upregulate the expression of miR-150 in human breast cancer MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Inhibition of the canonical WNT signaling pathway using the siRNA against β-catenin reduced the expression of miR-150 in the miR-142-expressing MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Moreover, inhibition of the canonical WNT signaling pathway using the siRNA against β-catenin reduced the expression of miR-150 in the miR-142-expressing MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The inhibition of miR-142 in human breast cancer organoids formed by human BCSCs infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentiviruses decreased the expression of miR-150.
source: We further confirmed that the inhibition of miR-142 in human breast cancer organoids formed by human BCSCs infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentiviruses decreased the expression of miR-150 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The upregulation of miR-142 induces the expression of miR-150 at least partially through the canonical WNT signaling pathway.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the upregulation of miR-142 induces the expression of miR-150 at least partially through the canonical WNT signaling pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the chromatin IP, real-time PCR, and knockdown experiments.

claim: Overall, 7 out of 12 transplants with non-infected mammary cells formed a mammary tree.
source: Overall, 7 out of 12 transplants with non-infected mammary cells and 7 out of 12 transplants with mammary cells infected with control lentivirus formed a mammary tree, suggesting that lentivirus infection was highly efficient and, by itself, did not perturb engraftment of mammary cells.
evidence: This is data from the mammary transplantation experiments.

claim: 7 out of 12 transplants with mammary cells infected with control lentivirus formed a mammary tree.
source: Overall, 7 out of 12 transplants with non-infected mammary cells and 7 out of 12 transplants with mammary cells infected with control lentivirus formed a mammary tree, suggesting that lentivirus infection was highly efficient and, by itself, did not perturb engraftment of mammary cells.
evidence: This is data from the mammary transplantation experiments.

claim: Lentivirus infection was highly efficient and did not perturb engraftment of mammary cells.
source: Overall, 7 out of 12 transplants with non-infected mammary cells and 7 out of 12 transplants with mammary cells infected with control lentivirus formed a mammary tree, suggesting that lentivirus infection was highly efficient and, by itself, did not perturb engraftment of mammary cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar engraftment rates between infected and non-infected cells.

claim: Mammary cells infected with control lentivirus showed the outgrowth of a normal-looking mammary tree structure consisting of single layers of myoepithelial and luminal cells.
source: Whole-mount staining and histological analysis of mammary fat pads injected with the control lentivirus-infected mammary cells showed the outgrowth of a normal-looking mammary tree structure consisting of single layers of myoepithelial and luminal cells (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount and histological images shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Mammary cells infected with the miR-142 lentivirus formed disorganized structures with multiple layers of cells.
source: In contrast, mammary cells infected with the miR-142 lentivirus formed disorganized structures with multiple layers of cells (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount and histological images shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: miR-142-expressing mammary cells formed clusters of cells with an abnormal appearance in which the normal mammary structure was disrupted because of the aberrant cell proliferation.
source: Histological analysis revealed that miR-142-expressing mammary cells formed clusters of cells with an abnormal appearance in which the normal mammary structure was disrupted because of the aberrant cell proliferation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Mammary cells infected with the miR-150-expressing lentivirus formed a hyperplastic mammary tree with extremely increased branching and thick mammary ducts.
source: Mammary cells infected with the miR-150-expressing lentivirus formed a hyperplastic mammary tree with extremely increased branching and thick mammary ducts (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is supported by whole-mount images and quantification shown in Figure 6A,C.

claim: miR-150-expressing mammary cells formed thick hyperplastic ducts with multiple layers of mammary cells, with scattered small cavities among mammary cell layers.
source: Histological analysis of the mammary trees showed that miR-150-expressing mammary cells formed thick hyperplastic ducts with multiple layers of mammary cells, with scattered small cavities among mammary cell layers (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Unlike miR-142-expressing mammary cells, miR-150-expressing mammary cells had a normal cellular appearance.
source: But unlike miR-142-expressing mammary cells, miR-150-expressing mammary cells had a normal cellular appearance.
evidence: This is observed from histological analysis.

claim: The epithelial cells in the miR-142-expressing and miR-150-expressing mammary tissues were positively stained with an anti-PCNA antibody.
source: To confirm that both the dysplastic mammary tissue formed by the miR-142-expressing mammary cells and the hyperplastic mammary tissue formed by the miR-150-expressing mammary cells were both hyperproliferative, we immunostained these tissues with an anti-PCNA antibody. We found that the epithelial cells in the miR-142-expressing and miR-150-expressing mammary tissues were positively stained with an anti-PCNA antibody (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The mammary tissue regenerated by the control lentivirus transfected mammary cells was rarely stained with an anti-PCNA antibody.
source: In contrast, the mammary tissue regenerated by the control lentivirus transfected mammary cells was rarely stained with an anti-PCNA antibody.
evidence: This is observed from immunohistochemistry.

claim: The enforced expression of either miR-142 or miR-150 induces hyperproliferation in the mammary tissues.
source: The results indicate that the enforced expression of either miR-142 or miR-150 induces hyperproliferation in the mammary tissues and that the phenotype of the miR-142-expressing mammary tissue is more severe and accompanied with abnormal morphology.
evidence: This is inferred from the PCNA staining and histological analysis.

claim: The phenotype of the miR-142-expressing mammary tissue is more severe and accompanied with abnormal morphology compared to miR-150-expressing tissue.
source: The results indicate that the enforced expression of either miR-142 or miR-150 induces hyperproliferation in the mammary tissues and that the phenotype of the miR-142-expressing mammary tissue is more severe and accompanied with abnormal morphology.
evidence: This is inferred from the histological comparison.

claim: Cytoplasmic and nuclear localization of β-catenin was observed in the dysplastic cell clusters formed by the mammary cells infected with the miR-142-expressing lentivirus.
source: While the signal for the β-catenin in mammary tissue formed by the control lentivirus-infected mammary cells was weakly detectable and its localization was mostly membranous, we observed cytoplasmic and nuclear localization of β-catenin and the positive staining of active β-catenin in the dysplastic cell clusters formed by the mammary cells infected with the miR-142-expressing lentivirus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Positive staining of active β-catenin was observed in the dysplastic cell clusters formed by the mammary cells infected with the miR-142-expressing lentivirus.
source: While the signal for the β-catenin in mammary tissue formed by the control lentivirus-infected mammary cells was weakly detectable and its localization was mostly membranous, we observed cytoplasmic and nuclear localization of β-catenin and the positive staining of active β-catenin in the dysplastic cell clusters formed by the mammary cells infected with the miR-142-expressing lentivirus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nuclear β-catenin was detectable in the miR-142-expressing mammary tissue because the WNT signaling pathway was highly overstimulated.
source: Although the immunohistochemistry of β-catenin in general suffers from non-specific staining, we detected nuclear β-catenin in the miR-142-expressing mammary tissue. We speculate that nuclear β-catenin was detectable in these immunohistochemistry experiments because the WNT signaling pathway was highly overstimulated in the miR-142-expressing mammary tissue.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation.

claim: miR-142 regulates the properties of mammary cells by activating the WNT signaling pathway and conferring the aberrant proliferative ability.
source: These results suggest that miR-142 regulates the properties of mammary cells by activating the WNT signaling pathway and conferring the aberrant proliferative ability.
evidence: This is inferred from the β-catenin localization and proliferation data.

claim: 94% of the human BCSCs were infected with the control lentivirus 2 days after the infection.
source: The flow cytometric analyses revealed that 94% and 96% of the human BCSCs were infected with the control or the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus, respectively, 2 days after the infection (data not shown).
evidence: This is data from flow cytometry analysis.

claim: 96% of the human BCSCs were infected with the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus 2 days after the infection.
source: The flow cytometric analyses revealed that 94% and 96% of the human BCSCs were infected with the control or the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing lentivirus, respectively, 2 days after the infection (data not shown).
evidence: This is data from flow cytometry analysis.

claim: The growth of the human breast cancer xenografts formed by the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing BCSCs was significantly slower than that of the control human breast cancer xenografts.
source: The growth of the human breast cancer xenografts formed by the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing BCSCs was significantly slower than that of the control human breast cancer xenografts (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The protein level of APC was elevated in the human breast cancer cells isolated from the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing breast cancer xenograft.
source: We further confirmed that consistent with the results of the human breast cancer cell lines (Figure 2), the protein level of APC was elevated in the human breast cancer cells isolated from the anti-miR-142-3p-expressing breast cancer xenograft (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The inhibition of miR-142-3p in human BCSCs elevated the expression of APC protein and suppressed the proliferation of the breast cancer cells in vivo.
source: These results suggest that the inhibition of miR-142-3p in human BCSCs from this patient elevated the expression of APC protein and suppressed the proliferation of the breast cancer cells in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the tumor growth and Western blot data.

claim: APC is indeed a relevant target of miR-142.
source: Our results demonstrate that APC is indeed a relevant target of miR-142.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: In both normal and malignant mammary cells, miR-142 activates the canonical WNT signaling pathway and regulates proliferation at least in part through upregulation of the WNT/β-catenin signaling.
source: In both normal and malignant mammary cells, miR-142 activates the canonical WNT signaling pathway and regulates proliferation at least in part through upregulation of the WNT/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Each miRNA can have hundreds of targets in general.
source: However, because each miRNA can have hundreds of targets in general, it is likely that other pathways also have roles in the regulation of normal and malignant breast epithelium by miR-142.
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNAs.

claim: It is likely that other pathways also have roles in the regulation of normal and malignant breast epithelium by miR-142.
source: However, because each miRNA can have hundreds of targets in general, it is likely that other pathways also have roles in the regulation of normal and malignant breast epithelium by miR-142.
evidence: This is speculation based on the general properties of miRNAs.

claim: Expression of APC protein is modulated by miRNAs, such as miR-135, miR-27, miR-155, and miR-142.
source: Expression of APC protein is modulated by miRNAs, such as miR-135, miR-27, miR-155, and miR-142 (Nagel et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2009; Wang and Xu, 2010; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Elevated expression of miR-135 has been observed in colorectal adenomas and adenocarcinomas with/without biallelic APC mutations.
source: Elevated expression of miR-135, which targets the APC mRNA, has been observed in colorectal adenomas and adenocarcinomas with/without biallelic APC mutations, suggesting that this miRNA could play a primary or synergistic role in activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway during colon cancer development (Nagel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: miR-135 could play a primary or synergistic role in activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway during colon cancer development.
source: Elevated expression of miR-135, which targets the APC mRNA, has been observed in colorectal adenomas and adenocarcinomas with/without biallelic APC mutations, suggesting that this miRNA could play a primary or synergistic role in activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway during colon cancer development (Nagel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: In a model of osteoblast differentiation, miR-27 and miR-142 were shown to regulate APC expression and to positively modulate the canonical WNT signaling pathway.
source: In a model of osteoblast differentiation, miR-27 and miR-142 were shown to regulate APC expression and to positively modulate the canonical WNT signaling pathway (Wang and Xu, 2010; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: miR-155 targets APC and inhibition of miR-155 using the anti-miR-155 increases the protein level of APC.
source: miR-155 targets APC and inhibition of miR-155 using the anti-miR-155 increases the protein level of APC (Lu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Both miR-142-3p and miR-155 are more highly expressed in the human BCSCs than in the NTG cells.
source: It is noteworthy that both miR-142-3p and miR-155 are more highly expressed in the human BCSCs than in the NTG cells (Shimono et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a previous finding supported by citation.

claim: miR-142 reduced the protein level of APC and enhanced the canonical WNT signaling pathway in normal and malignant mammary epithelium.
source: In this study, we show that miR-142 reduced the protein level of APC and enhanced the canonical WNT signaling pathway in normal and malignant mammary epithelium.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The canonical WNT signaling pathway is important for the stem cells in the mammary gland.
source: This is important for the stem cells in the mammary gland (Haegebarth and Clevers, 2009; Zeng and Nusse, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The dysregulated WNT signaling can enhance niche independence and promote aberrant proliferation of stem cells.
source: The dysregulated WNT signaling can enhance niche independence and promote aberrant proliferation of stem cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of WNT signaling in stem cells.

claim: Upregulation of miR-142, miR-150, and miR-155 may not only be hallmarks of BCSCs but could actually contribute directly to aberrant proliferation of these cells.
source: Taken together, upregulation of miR-142, miR-150, and miR-155 may not only be hallmarks of BCSCs but could actually contribute directly to aberrant proliferation of these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional studies.

claim: miR-150 is a target of miR-142 via its regulation of the canonical WNT/β-catenin signaling.
source: In this report, we show that miR-150 is a target of miR-142 via its regulation of the canonical WNT/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: miR-150 plays a role in the proliferation induced by miR-142 and the canonical WNT/β-catenin signaling.
source: Notably, miR-150 plays a role in the proliferation induced by miR-142 and the canonical WNT/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional studies.

claim: miR-150's regulation of proliferation is downstream of the canonical WNT/β-catenin signaling.
source: Our results suggest that miR-150's regulation of proliferation is downstream of the canonical WNT/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing miR-142 activates WNT signaling which then induces miR-150.

claim: The APC mRNA has a predicted target site for miR-150.
source: In addition, the APC mRNA has a predicted target site for miR-150.
evidence: This is stated as a computational prediction.

claim: The activity of the luciferase plasmid containing the miR-150 target site within the 3′ UTR of the APC mRNA was reduced by 32% when the miR-150 precursor was co-transfected.
source: We constructed the pGL3 luciferase expression plasmid in which the miR-150 target site within the 3′ UTR of the APC mRNA was cloned downstream of a luciferase minigene and found that the activity of this luciferase plasmid was reduced by 32% when the miR-150 precursor was co-transfected (data not shown).
evidence: This is data from a luciferase assay.

claim: The presence of many other target genes with higher affinity to the miR-150-containing RISC will perturb the ability of miR-150 to regulate the APC mRNA.
source: Because each miRNA has multiple target genes, we speculate that the presence of many other target genes with higher affinity to the miR-150-containing RISC will perturb the ability of miR-150 to regulate the APC mRNA and that miR-150 has much weaker effect, if any, on the WNT signaling pathway in vivo.
evidence: This is speculation based on the Ago IP/microarray results and general miRNA biology.

claim: miR-150 has much weaker effect, if any, on the WNT signaling pathway in vivo.
source: Because each miRNA has multiple target genes, we speculate that the presence of many other target genes with higher affinity to the miR-150-containing RISC will perturb the ability of miR-150 to regulate the APC mRNA and that miR-150 has much weaker effect, if any, on the WNT signaling pathway in vivo.
evidence: This is speculation based on the Ago IP/microarray results.

claim: Some miRNAs are known to be regulated by transcriptional factors which have critical roles in regulating development, proliferation, and cell survival.
source: Some miRNAs are known to be regulated by transcriptional factors which have critical roles in regulating development, proliferation, and cell survival (Bracken et al., 2008; O'Donnell et al., 2005; Raver-Shapira et al., 2007; Yamakuchi et al., 2010; Chang et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The transcriptional repressors, ZEB1 and ZEB2, suppress transcription of the miR-200a-miR-200b-miR-429 cluster, which in turn represses expression of ZEB1 and ZEB2, thereby forming a double negative feedback loop.
source: For example, the transcriptional repressors, ZEB1 and ZEB2, which can play a positive role in EMT, suppress transcription of the miR-200a-miR-200b-miR-429 cluster, which in turn represses expression of ZEB1 and ZEB2, thereby forming a double negative feedback loop (Bracken et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: c-Myc enhances expression of the miR-17-92 cluster, which in turn represses E2F1 expression and thereby suppresses cell-cycle entry.
source: c-Myc enhances expression of the miR-17-92 cluster, which in turn represses E2F1 expression and thereby suppresses cell-cycle entry (O'Donnell et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The tumor suppressor Tp53 regulates expression of miRNAs, including miR-34a, miR-107, and miR-200.
source: The tumor suppressor Tp53 regulates expression of miRNAs, including miR-34a, miR-107, and miR-200 (Chang et al., 2007; Raver-Shapira et al., 2007; Yamakuchi et al., 2010; Chang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Expression of miR-10b is regulated by the transcription factor Twist.
source: Expression of miR-10b, a miRNA that promotes breast cancer cell metastasis by inhibiting HoxD10, is regulated by the transcription factor Twist, a major regulator of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Ma et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: miR-10b promotes breast cancer cell metastasis by inhibiting HoxD10.
source: Expression of miR-10b, a miRNA that promotes breast cancer cell metastasis by inhibiting HoxD10, is regulated by the transcription factor Twist, a major regulator of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Ma et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A TCF/β-catenin binding site exists in the promoter region of miR-150.
source: We identified a TCF/β-catenin binding site in the promoter region of miR-150 and showed that miR-142 stimulates the canonical WNT signaling pathway in vivo and elevates the expression of miR-150.
evidence: This is supported by the chromatin IP data.

claim: miR-142 stimulates the canonical WNT signaling pathway in vivo and elevates the expression of miR-150.
source: We identified a TCF/β-catenin binding site in the promoter region of miR-150 and showed that miR-142 stimulates the canonical WNT signaling pathway in vivo and elevates the expression of miR-150.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: miR-150 induces proliferation and suppresses apoptosis of breast cancer cells.
source: It has recently been reported that miR-150 induces proliferation and suppresses apoptosis of breast cancer cells (Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Suppression of the APC protein expression by miR-142 increases the activity of the canonical WNT signaling pathway and thereby enhances the miR-150 expression.
source: A simple model to explain the upregulation of miR-142 and miR-150 in human BCSCs is that suppression of the APC protein expression by miR-142 increases the activity of the canonical WNT signaling pathway and thereby enhances the miR-150 expression.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the study's findings.

claim: miR-142 upregulates the expression of miR-150 when miR-142 is highly expressed and/or the WNT signaling pathway is strongly stimulated in mammary epithelial cells.
source: We note that our results show that miR-142 upregulates the expression of miR-150 when miR-142 is highly expressed and/or the WNT signaling pathway is strongly stimulated in mammary epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings with context.

claim: miR-142 is highly expressed in human BCSCs but weakly expressed or undetectable in the stem/progenitor population of the mammary epithelial cells.
source: Considering that miR-142 is highly expressed in human BCSCs but weakly expressed or undetectable in the stem/progenitor population of the mammary epithelial cells, our result suggests that the upregulation of miR-142 and the increase of the miR-150 expression by miR-142 could be especially relevant in the initiation and/or progression of human breast cancers driven by human BCSCs in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from previous work.

claim: The upregulation of miR-142 and the increase of the miR-150 expression by miR-142 could be especially relevant in the initiation and/or progression of human breast cancers driven by human BCSCs in vivo.
source: Considering that miR-142 is highly expressed in human BCSCs but weakly expressed or undetectable in the stem/progenitor population of the mammary epithelial cells, our result suggests that the upregulation of miR-142 and the increase of the miR-150 expression by miR-142 could be especially relevant in the initiation and/or progression of human breast cancers driven by human BCSCs in vivo.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the study's findings.

claim: Mice heterozygous for a germline mutation in Apc (Apc+/850T, ApcMin mice) spontaneously develop mammary tumors.
source: Mice heterozygous for a germline mutation in Apc (Apc+/850T, ApcMin mice) spontaneously develop mammary tumors, although at significantly lower frequency than intestinal tumors (Moser et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mice heterozygous for a C-terminal truncation mutation, Apc+/1572T, develop multifocal mammary tumors with pulmonary metastasis at much higher frequency.
source: Mice heterozygous for a C-terminal truncation mutation, Apc+/1572T, develop multifocal mammary tumors with pulmonary metastasis at much higher frequency (Gaspar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MMTV-promoter-Wnt1 transgenic mice develop breast tumors composed of both luminal and myoepithelial component and expanded mammary stem cell pools.
source: MMTV-promoter-Wnt1 transgenic mice develop breast tumors composed of both luminal and myoepithelial component and expanded mammary stem cell pools (Cho et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Heterozygous mutation of APC in immature, but not mature, mammary epithelium induces breast tumors.
source: Finally, heterozygous mutation of APC in immature, but not mature, mammary epithelium induces breast tumors (Kuraguchi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway in mammary epithelium contributes to mammary tumor initiation in mouse models.
source: These results suggest that activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway in mammary epithelium, by mutation of APC, excessive ectopic WNT expression, and/or stabilization of β-catenin contribute to mammary tumor initiation in the same way as colon cancer at least in mouse models of the mammary tumors.
evidence: This is inferred from the mouse model studies cited.

claim: APC mutations are less frequently found in human breast cancers compared to mouse models.
source: However, although these mouse models that upregulate the canonical WNT signaling activity induce mammary gland tumors (Moser et al., 1993; Gaspar et al., 2009; Kuraguchi et al., 2009), APC mutations are less frequently found in human breast cancers (Furuuchi et al., 2000; Jin et al., 2001; Sarrio et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: APC has additional important cellular functions, including roles in cell adhesion, migration, organization of actin and microtubule networks, spindle formation, and chromosome segregation.
source: In addition, APC has additional important cellular functions, including roles in cell adhesion, migration, organization of actin and microtubule networks, spindle formation, and chromosome segregation (Aoki and Taketo, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Dysregulation of APC functions by mutations in the APC gene is frequently implicated in tumor initiation and progression.
source: Thus, dysregulation of these processes by mutations in the APC gene is frequently implicated in tumor initiation and progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the known functions of APC.

claim: Upregulation of miR-142 can significantly enhance the canonical WNT signaling pathway through the suppression of APC including in the mammary cells.
source: Our results show that upregulation of miR-142 can significantly enhance the canonical WNT signaling pathway through the suppression of APC including in the mammary cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: miR-142 could provide at least a part of the shared molecular mechanism for aberrant activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway in BCSCs and for the initiation and progression of breast cancers.
source: Therefore, miR-142, a miRNA frequently upregulated in human BCSCs than in the NTG cells (Shimono et al., 2009), could provide at least a part of the shared molecular mechanism for aberrant activation of the canonical WNT signaling pathway in BCSCs and for the initiation and progression of breast cancers.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the study's findings.
